title: Build Reusable Prompts and a Personal Prompt Library

thumbnail.headline: Save Prompts That Work
thumbnail.image: Navy background, a small library shelf of labelled prompt cards with one card pulled out showing empty fill-in spaces, headline in teal Inter Bold.

slide.title: Save Prompts That Work
slide.body: Shelf of index cards labelled 'Weekly update', 'Supplier reminder', 'Meeting agenda'; one card shows a template with empty brackets. Small tag: AI for Everyday Work · Lesson 11.

production_notes: [VERSION] Features for saving instructions or projects inside AI tools, and which plans include them, must be checked before recording. The voiceover only says 'some AI tools also let you save instructions inside the tool; check what your plan offers'.
[REGION] Employer rules on where work files and prompt libraries may be stored differ by organisation and country; the voiceover tells learners to follow their own policy.
Sione and his Suva hotel are hypothetical; no real hotel name or logo in stock footage.
The template and Sione's prompts appear in full on code-layout slides (scenes 3, 10 and 11). The square brackets are on the slides only; the presenter describes them as spaces to fill in.

Hook.voiceover: Last month you wrote a prompt that gave you a perfect weekly report. This week, you cannot remember how you wrote it, so you start again from zero. A small personal prompt library solves this problem.

Explain.voiceover: In the last lesson, you mapped three of your tasks. Now we write the prompts for them. A reusable prompt is a prompt you save and use again, with spaces to fill in for the details that change each time. It follows the four parts from lesson two.

slide.title: Reusable prompts
slide.body: Save once · fill in the gaps · reuse every week

Explain.voiceover: Here is a simple template. Task, what you want. Reader, who will read it and what they need. Context, the key facts for this week, with no personal data. Format, the length, structure and tone. And example, a past version you liked, with names removed.

slide.title: A reusable prompt template
slide.body:
Task: [what you want: write / rewrite / summarise / list]
Reader: [who will read it and what they need]
Context: [the key facts for this week, no personal data]
Format: [length, structure, tone]
Example: [paste a past version you liked, with names removed]

Explain.voiceover: The spaces in brackets change each week. Everything else stays the same. You fill in the gaps, paste it into your AI assistant, and get a consistent result.

slide.title: Fixed parts and changing parts
slide.body: Template with fixed lines in navy and the bracketed spaces glowing teal, labelled 'changes each week'.

Explain.voiceover: The first version of a prompt rarely gives the best result. So test it, look at what went wrong, and change the prompt, not just the output. If the answer was too long, add a word limit. If the tone was too formal, ask for a friendly tone.

slide.title: Fix the prompt, not just the output
slide.body: Too long → add 'maximum 150 words'. Too formal → add 'friendly, like a message to a colleague'.

Explain.voiceover: If it invented details, tell it to use only the facts you give, and to write missing instead of guessing. If it forgot a section, add that heading to the format line. After two or three rounds, the prompt is usually reliable for that task.

slide.title: Fix the prompt, not just the output
slide.body: Invented details → 'Use only the facts I give you. If something is missing, write [MISSING].' Forgot a section → add the heading to the Format line.

Explain.voiceover: Where should you keep your library? A simple document or notes file is enough. Give each prompt a clear name. Store only the template with empty spaces, never a filled-in version with names or figures. Keep it where your employer allows work files, and follow your employer's AI policy. Some AI tools also let you save instructions inside the tool, so check what your plan offers.

slide.title: Your prompt library
slide.body: A simple document or notes file · Clear names: 'Weekly status update', 'Supplier reminder' · Templates only, never filled-in versions · Stored where your employer allows

Explain.voiceover: Think of a recipe book. You do not invent a new recipe every time you cook the same dish. You follow the version that worked, change the ingredients for today, and note any improvement in the margin.
Explain.stock_query: handwritten recipe book notes in margin

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's build one. Sione is a front office supervisor at a hotel in Suva, in Fiji. Every Monday, he writes a short update for the hotel manager about the week before.
Demonstrate.stock_query: hotel front desk supervisor tropical hotel

Demonstrate.voiceover: His first prompt just asks for a weekly update about the front office. The result is generic, and it invents figures.

slide.title: Sione's first prompt
slide.body: Write a weekly update for my manager about the front office.

Demonstrate.voiceover: So he builds a reusable prompt. The task is a weekly front office update. The reader is the hotel manager, who wants a quick overview. The context is a space for this week's facts. The format has three headings: highlights, problems and next week, in one hundred and fifty words or fewer. And one clear rule: use only the facts I give you.

slide.title: Sione's reusable prompt
slide.body:
Task: Write a weekly front office update.
Reader: The hotel manager, who wants a quick overview.
Context: [3 to 5 bullet points of this week's facts]
Format: 3 headings (Highlights, Problems, Next week), maximum 150 words, plain and direct.
Use only the facts I give you. Do not add numbers.

Demonstrate.voiceover: He tests it with last week's notes, with guest names removed. The result is good, but the problems section sounds too negative. So he adds neutral tone, focus on solutions, to the format line. The second result is right.

slide.title: Test and improve
slide.body: Test 1: 'Problems' section too negative (amber) → Fix: add 'neutral tone, focus on solutions' → Test 2: right (green tick).

Demonstrate.voiceover: He saves the template in his work notes file, under the name weekly manager update, with the context line left empty. Next Monday, he only needs to add the new facts.

slide.title: Saved to the library
slide.body: Name: Weekly manager update · Context line left empty · Saved in his work notes file

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to save prompts that already contain one week's details, such as client names or prices. Then your library becomes a store of confidential data. Save templates, not filled-in versions.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, a reusable prompt keeps the task, reader and format fixed, and leaves spaces for the facts that change. Second, improve a prompt by fixing the prompt itself after each test, for example with a length limit or a do not guess rule. Third, keep your library in an approved place and free of confidential data.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Fixed task, reader, format; spaces for facts. 2. Test, then fix the prompt itself. 3. Approved place, no confidential data.

CTA.voiceover: This is capstone step two. In the exercise below this video, write a reusable prompt for each of your three tasks. Test each one with this week's facts, with names removed, check the result, and improve the prompt at least once. The last lesson is Measure Time Saved and Present Your Redesign. See you there.
